`case_study:worldcom-2002` | 2002-07-21 | tickers: US-WCOEQ | confidence: verified

WorldCom grew via ~60 acquisitions (MCI for ~$37 bn in 1998); stock peaked ~$64 in mid-1999 and the company filed for bankruptcy on 21 Jul 2002 (then the largest US bankruptcy, ~$107 bn assets). In Jun 2002 internal auditor Cynthia Cooper's team found >$3.8 bn of line costs (fees paid to other carriers) improperly capitalised as capex in 2001-Q1 2002; the total misstatement grew to ~$11 bn including reserve releases. CEO Bernie Ebbers (who had borrowed ~$400 m from the company to avoid selling pledged shares) got 25 years. Visible flags: (1) the line-cost/revenue (E/R) ratio held steady ~42% while the telecom industry's pricing collapsed -- 'too smooth'; (2) capex and PP&E rising while revenue growth stalled (aggressive capitalisation shows in asset-quality and depreciation ratios); (3) serial acquisitions with merger reserves that could be released into earnings; (4) huge loans to the CEO secured by pledged stock; (5) CFO vs net income gap widened when the 'capex' was stripped out. Lesson: capitalising operating costs is the simplest way to inflate EBITDA and CFO simultaneously -- check capex/sales and capex vs depreciation trends against peers; roll-ups with merger reserves are low-quality earnings.

**Lesson:** Capitalised opex inflates both EBITDA and CFO; watch capex intensity
**Spotted early by:** internal audit (Cynthia Cooper)

`person:kenneth-andrade` | confidence: **single-source** | tags: india, process, contrarian, cyclical, midcap

Ran IDFC Premier Equity from Oct 2005 to Sept 2015 (earlier Kotak Mahindra AMC); a FLAME University bio cites ~22.3% CAGR over ten years for the flagship (promotional, unverified end date). The fund became so popular that inflows were restricted (characterisation); after his 2015 exit it struggled. Founded Old Bridge Capital in 2015 (PMS, ~Rs 8,000 crore AUM per a Mint interview); launched the Old Bridge Focused Equity MF in Jan 2024. Process edge: supply-side, capital-cycle analysis - buy into industries where capacity additions have stopped, weak players are exiting and the survivors ('last man standing') gain pricing power; favour high asset-turnover, capital-light businesses; go where earnings are depressed and nobody is looking. Mistakes: his contrarian, commodity/cyclical-leaning PMS lagged in 2016-2020 when quality-growth dominated (characterisation; check data); the mid-cap-heavy IDFC fund suffered as it grew large. Copyable: track industry capex and capacity utilisation (cement, paper, sugar, chemicals) - consolidation plus no new capacity is an early signal that tends to precede margin recovery by 1-2 years; avoid sectors where everyone is announcing capacity.

body:
`insight:false-alarm-vs-trap-lessons` · single-source

From 17 false-alarm and 14 hidden-trap cases (India 21, US/global 10): (1) VERIFIABILITY OUTSIDE THE ACCOUNTS: every false alarm had a mechanism an outsider could check independently: store counts and footfall (DMart, Trent), subscribers/engagement (Netflix, Bharti), gold prices and owned-store inventory (Titan), sovereign counterparty and order book (HAL), listed investee prices (Info Edge), deliveries/factory output (Tesla). Every trap's good number could only be checked through company-supplied data (Satyam cash, Wirecard TPAs, Luckin orders, Manpasand distributors, Gitanjali group receivables). (2) CASH EVENTUALLY ARRIVED in false alarms (HAL FY21, Bharti CFO Rs 1.22 lakh cr, Netflix FCF 2020+, Reliance stake sales); in traps, cash never arrived or vanished. (3) GOVERNANCE was clean or improving in false alarms (Bharti, Tata/Titan, Bajaj, Apollo reducing pledge); traps carried governance flags (auditor exits, promoter stake falls, related-party deals, regulator action). (4) WHO TOOK THE OTHER SIDE: false-alarm dilution was bought by strong investors or the promoter; trap capital came from short-term lenders/MFs. (5) MANY FALSE ALARMS WERE ONLY HALF FALSE: high P/E stopped working at ~2x own median (DMart, Asian Paints, Pidilite, Page, Bajaj Finance, HDFC Bank all had 4-6 flat years after peak multiples) and Reliance's low ROCE capped returns. So 'flag false for the business' and 'flag false for the price' are separate verdicts. (6) Our checklist would have wrongly rejected Titan (CFO/PAT 0.62), Apollo (pledge) and HAL (receivables), and wrongly passed Vakrangee on CFO/PAT: calibrate, don't abandon.
